core: working definition: public health is the science and practice of protecting and improving the health of populations (CDC/APHA tradition)
prevention over cure: public health works to prevent problems before they start, with an original example
the population lens: whole communities, not single patients; individual-health-versus-population-health is a sibling topic
classic wins: vaccines (smallpox eradication), clean water and sanitation (typhoid/cholera), motor-vehicle safety (seat belts)
who does it: health departments, researchers, epidemiologists, community health workers, and the broader workforce
public health and medicine: complementary, different tools
honest framing: public health is the work that disappears when it succeeds
supporting: CDC 10 Essential Public Health Services framework as the field's activity list
CDC figures: lifespan lengthened more than 30 years since 1900, about 25 years attributable to public health; life expectancy 47.3 (1900) to 76.8 (2000)
seat belt and child safety seat legislation: 49 states + DC adult seat belt laws, all 50 states + DC child passenger protection
APHA list of public health professionals and examples of public health work
MMWR achievements lists (1900-1999 and 2001-2010) as the factual record for the classic wins
outOfScope: population health as a concept (owned by public-health:foundations:population-health)
epidemiology methods and measures (owned by public-health:foundations:epidemiology)
the prevention spectrum and primary/secondary/tertiary levels (owned by public-health:foundations:prevention)

claims.claim: Public health is the science and practice of protecting and improving the health of populations: the CDC's 10 Essential Public Health Services describe public health as the activities all communities should undertake to protect and promote the health of all people in all communities, and APHA describes it as promoting and protecting the health of all people and their communities.
Public health aims to prevent people from getting sick or injured in the first place, while the health care industry treats people who are sick.
Public health focuses on entire populations, while health care focuses on individual patients.

Vaccination has resulted in the eradication of smallpox, elimination of poliomyelitis in the Americas, and control of measles, rubella, tetanus, diphtheria, Haemophilus influenzae type b, and other infectious diseases in the United States and other parts of the world.

Control of infectious diseases resulted from clean water and improved sanitation; waterborne typhoid and cholera, major causes of illness and death early in the 20th century, were reduced dramatically.

Improvements in motor-vehicle safety — safer vehicles and highways plus behavior change such as increased use of seat belts, child safety seats, and motorcycle helmets — contributed to large reductions in motor-vehicle-related deaths; by the 2000s, 49 states and DC had seat belt laws for adults and all 50 states and DC had legislation protecting children riding in vehicles.

Since 1900 the average lifespan of persons in the United States has lengthened by more than 30 years, with about 25 years of that gain attributable to advances in public health; life expectancy at birth rose from 47.3 years in 1900 to 76.8 in 2000.

Public health is carried out by a broad workforce — including epidemiologists, community health workers, health educators, scientists and researchers, inspectors, and public health physicians and nurses — organized around essential services such as assessing and monitoring population health, investigating health problems and hazards, informing and educating people, mobilizing communities, and building a skilled workforce.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Public health versus medicine as a clean split
positions: APHA frames the split simply: health care treats people who are sick, public health prevents illness and focuses on entire populations
In practice the two overlap: clinicians also prevent (screenings, vaccines), and the EPHS framework includes assuring equitable access to individual services and care
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Lesson presents the simple APHA-style distinction and explicitly notes the two are complementary partners; the boundary nuances belong to the sibling lesson on individual health versus population health.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Attribution of lifespan gains to public health
positions: MMWR 1999 attributes roughly 25 of the 30+ years of lifespan gain since 1900 to advances in public health
Any such attribution is an estimate; medical care, economic growth, and other factors also contributed
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Lesson states the figure as the CDC reported it, with the source named, and does not overstate it.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The 'work that disappears when it succeeds' framing
positions: Prevention success is invisible — no outbreak, no headlines — which is the lesson's honest framing
Some public health successes are visible (vaccination campaigns, seat belt laws), and some failures are silent and slow
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Presented as the lesson's interpretive honest-framing section, consistent with the source material, not as an attributed quotation.
